title: California Homeowners Insurance: What Buyers Need to Know Now
description: Finding homeowners insurance in California has gotten harder. Learn why, what the FAIR Plan is, and how buyers can shop early to keep their closing on track.
image_alt: A gray wooden house with a front porch and trees

faq.q: Do I need homeowners insurance to get a mortgage?
faq.a: Yes. Lenders require proof of adequate homeowners insurance before funding the loan.

faq.q: What is the California FAIR Plan?
faq.a: It's California's insurer of last resort, offering basic fire coverage to property owners who can't find coverage in the traditional market. It's often paired with a separate policy for other coverages.

faq.q: When should I start shopping for insurance as a buyer?
faq.a: As early as possible, ideally before or right after your offer is accepted, especially for homes in higher wildfire-risk areas.

body_html:
A few years ago, homeowners insurance was a box buyers checked in the last week of escrow. Not anymore. In California, insurance has become one of the most important early steps in a home purchase, and in some areas it can affect whether a deal closes on time.

What changed

After years of costly wildfire seasons and rising rebuilding costs, many traditional insurers raised premiums, tightened where they'll write new policies, or pulled back from higher-risk areas. As a result, more homeowners have turned to the California FAIR Plan, the state's insurer of last resort. According to KQED's reporting, FAIR Plan enrollment has grown substantially in recent years, and the plan announced an average rate increase taking effect in the fall of 2026, with the largest increases in high wildfire-risk areas.

State regulators have been working on reforms intended to bring more private insurers back into the market. The California Department of Insurance is the best source for current updates and consumer resources.

Why insurance matters to your loan

Lenders require proof of adequate coverage before funding. Your insurance premium is also part of your monthly housing payment, which affects your debt-to-income ratio. A much higher premium than expected can change what you qualify for, or how comfortable the payment feels.

Understanding the FAIR Plan

The FAIR Plan generally provides basic fire coverage. Homeowners who use it often add a separate "difference in conditions" policy to cover things like liability, theft, and water damage that the FAIR Plan doesn't. Together, the two policies can cost more than a traditional policy, so budget accordingly.

Coverage pathWhat it typically includes
Traditional homeowners policyDwelling, other structures, personal property, liability, loss of use
FAIR PlanPrimarily fire-related coverage for the structure
Difference in conditions policyFills gaps when paired with the FAIR Plan

How buyers can stay ahead

  1. Shop insurance before you fall in love with a house, especially in canyon, hillside, or wildland-adjacent neighborhoods.
  2. Ask the seller for their current premium and carrier. It's a useful starting point, though your quote may differ.
  3. Work with an independent agent or broker who can check multiple carriers.
  4. Get quotes in the first days of escrow and bind coverage well before closing.
  5. Ask about mitigation discounts. Home hardening and defensible space improvements may lower premiums with some carriers.

Features that can affect your quote

  • Wildfire risk score for the location
  • Roof age and material
  • Distance to fire hydrants and fire stations
  • Age of electrical, plumbing, and heating systems
  • Prior claims on the property

Your home inspection can surface issues, like an older roof, that matter to insurers. Read it with insurance in mind.

For condo buyers

Condo buyers have two layers: the HOA's master policy and your own interior policy. Lenders review the master policy as part of the condo approval. If the HOA's coverage has changed or lapsed, it can affect financing, so ask early.

Treat insurance like the appraisal: something to get moving in week one, not a final-week formality.

What insurance means for your monthly payment

Insurance usually becomes part of your monthly mortgage payment through an escrow, or impound, account. Your lender collects a portion of the annual premium each month along with property taxes and pays the bills when they're due. At closing, you'll typically prepay the first year's premium and fund a cushion in the escrow account.

Because premiums can change at renewal, your monthly payment can change too, even with a fixed-rate loan. Your servicer reviews the escrow account each year and adjusts the payment if taxes or insurance went up. When budgeting, it's wise to leave some room for increases rather than assuming today's premium will hold forever.

Questions to ask your insurance agent

  1. Which carriers are currently writing new policies in this ZIP code?
  2. Will this home need the FAIR Plan, and if so, what supplemental policy do you recommend?
  3. What deductible options are available, and how do they affect the premium?
  4. Does the quote include replacement cost coverage, and is the dwelling limit adequate to rebuild?
  5. Are there discounts for home hardening, newer roofs, or alarm systems?
  6. How long will it take to bind coverage once I'm in escrow?

Ask for the quote in writing and share it with your loan officer early. If the premium is higher than expected, it's far better to know before contingencies are removed than after. In some cases buyers renegotiate, adjust their budget, or choose a different property once they see the real insurance cost.

Finally, keep the policy information handy for closing. Your escrow officer and lender will need the declarations page, the premium amount, and the lender's name listed correctly as mortgagee. Small errors on those documents are an avoidable source of delays.

Insurance and your contingency timeline

California purchase contracts don't always include a separate insurance contingency, so think about how insurance fits into your existing contingency periods. If a quote comes back far higher than expected after you've removed contingencies, your options narrow. Getting a firm quote before your loan and inspection contingencies expire gives you room to make an informed decision.

The takeaway

Insurance in California requires more planning than it used to. Shop early, budget for the real premium, understand whether you'll need the FAIR Plan plus supplemental coverage, and keep your loan officer informed. Handled early, it's just one more checklist item. Left until the end, it's one of the most common causes of escrow delays in the state.
